clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant spondylometaphyseal dysplasia that is typically normal at birth and presents in early childhood with progressive short-trunk short stature and a waddling gait.
Caused by heterozygous, usually gain-of-function variants in TRPV4; many cases arise de novo, though dominant transmission occurs.

The radiographic hallmark is generalised platyspondyly with characteristically 'overfaced' (oversized) pedicles, together with prominent metaphyseal irregularity that is most marked at the proximal femora.
Delayed and dysplastic ossification of the femoral capital epiphyses can closely mimic bilateral Perthes disease or a metaphyseal chondrodysplasia.
Progressive kyphoscoliosis and pectus carinatum are common, so early spinal surveillance is important.

TRPV4 is strikingly pleiotropic: the allelic skeletal spectrum runs from autosomal dominant brachyolmia through this condition to spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia (Maroteaux type) and metatropic dysplasia, while other TRPV4 variants cause neuromuscular disease such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 2C and scapuloperoneal or congenital spinal muscular atrophy.
Intelligence and lifespan are typically normal, with morbidity being predominantly orthopaedic.
Cervical spine involvement can occur, so instability should be assessed before anaesthesia or spinal manipulation.
reference.pathophysiology: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, Kozlowski type is caused by heterozygous, typically gain-of-function variants in TRPV4, which encodes a calcium-permeable transient receptor potential cation channel expressed in chondrocytes. Enhanced or dysregulated channel activity alters intracellular calcium signalling, chondrocyte differentiation and the tempo of endochondral ossification, producing platyspondyly, metaphyseal irregularity and dysplastic femoral capital epiphyses. TRPV4 is remarkably pleiotropic: variants distributed along a genotype-phenotype continuum cause a family of skeletal dysplasias — autosomal dominant brachyolmia, this Kozlowski condition, spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia of the Maroteaux type and metatropic dysplasia — as well as distinct peripheral neuropathies and motor neuronopathies, so the same gene can generate either bone or nerve disease depending on the specific allele.
additionalDifferentials: Other spondylometaphyseal dysplasias (for example the corner-fracture / Sutcliffe type)
Spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia (including the allelic TRPV4 Maroteaux type)
Autosomal dominant brachyolmia (the milder allelic TRPV4 phenotype)
additionalInvestigations: Full skeletal survey covering spine, pelvis and metaphyses
TRPV4 sequencing or a skeletal dysplasia gene panel
Standing spine radiographs to detect and monitor scoliosis and kyphosis
Hip imaging to assess the femoral capital epiphyses
Growth monitoring with segmental (trunk-to-limb) disproportion measurements
Cervical spine imaging where instability is suspected
Genetic counselling addressing autosomal dominant inheritance and de novo occurrence
redFlags: Cervical instability with risk of cord compression
Restrictive respiratory compromise from chest and spinal deformity
reference.prognosis: Intelligence and lifespan are generally normal; individuals have disproportionate short-trunk short stature with orthopaedic complications including scoliosis, hip disease and early osteoarthritis.
pitfalls: Labelling the femoral head changes as bilateral Perthes disease and missing the underlying dysplasia
Assuming an autosomal recessive metaphyseal disorder rather than a dominant TRPV4 condition
Underestimating cervical spine instability before anaesthesia
Failing to recognise the wider TRPV4 spectrum, including neuromuscular phenotypes, when counselling
references: International nosology and classification of genetic skeletal disorders
Standard clinical genetics and dysmorphology reference texts
management: No disease-modifying drug therapy exists; care is orthopaedic and supportive, centred on the platyspondyly, hip dysplasia and disproportionate short stature
Regular standing spinal radiographic surveillance for progressive kyphoscoliosis and pectus carinatum, with bracing or corrective spinal fusion when curves progress
Orthopaedic management of hip disease, including osteotomy and later joint replacement for painful dysplastic femoral capital epiphyses and early osteoarthritis
Monitor for cervical spine instability, with imaging and surgical stabilisation if there is threat to the cord
Physiotherapy, analgesia and mobility aids to address the waddling gait, joint pain and functional limitation
Multidisciplinary input from clinical genetics, paediatric orthopaedics, spinal surgery and physiotherapy
Genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant TRPV4 disorder, discussing frequent de novo occurrence and family testing
